newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia cabinet to press on with budget cuts - Kudrin.
newsitem.headline: Russia cabinet to press on with budget cuts - Kudrin.

text.p: A top Russian government official reiterated on Thursday that the cabinet was ready to cut budget spending even if parliament failed to back the unpopular move, RIA news agency said.

RIA quoted first deputy Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin as saying that the government did not insist that the communist-dominated State Duma lower house formally approve its bill on cutting spending by 20 percent due to poor tax revenues.
"Judging by debates in the chamber the deputies are likely to let the cabinet make the cuts and later approve them in parliament," Kudrin said.

"If the deputes say a resolute 'no' to the bill we are ready to cut spending without parliamentary approval," he added. "But then they should make appropriate changes to the budget legislation. We are ready for either option."

Kudrin argued that budget cuts were inevitable to focus available resources on solving burning social problems, such as paying delayed pensions and wages to employees of state-run companies and public services.

In a clear sign of reluctance to take up the painful issue of budget cuts, the Duma's budget committee asked the government earlier on Thursday to withdraw its tough bill and said deputies should consider alternative ideas.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted Duma deputies as saying that the chamber, which is dominated by communists and other conservatives, should consider an alternative plan put forward by a group of deputies when it debates the issue on Friday.

It was not clear what alternatives the budget committee was talking about, but many deputies are attracted by the idea of doubling money supply, viewing it as a way to pay off wage arrears and easing the financial pains of the population.

Ministers and central bank officials say boosting the money supply would only rekindle inflation and they have rejected the idea, which is also opposed by some economic experts in the Communist Party -- the main backer of the idea.
A Duma vote would not be binding on the government.

Ministers, taking comfort from vague phrasing in the budget law -- which says the government must submit new spending plans to parliament but does not say that parliament must approve the plans -- are likely to ignore the Duma.
"We are happy if the Duma approves sequestration (cuts) it's alright if they reject it. The cuts will go ahead anyway," First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said on Wednesday.

The government, worried that dismal tax revenues have made a mockery of figures underpinning the 1997 budget, has already ordered ministries to cut spending and is telling ministries not to order goods which they cannot afford to pay for.
It wants the Duma to approve its decision to slash over 100 trillion roubles ($17.4 billion), effectively approving a new "realistic" budget. Deputies are likely to vote on the issue on Friday.
If parliament is not prepared to back the cuts, the government wants a law making clear that it has a free hand.
